catalog_quote: Stress – a combination of duration, intensity, and pitch resulting in ‘phonetic prominence’ or ‘acoustic salience’ (Ladd 2008: 61) – usually falls on the penultimate syllable of a word in Torau, for example ˈa.te ‘water’, ta.ˈbu.ni ‘place’. Secondary stress occurs on every second syllable preceding the penultimate syllable, for example ˌgi.go.ˈwe.le ‘whirlpool’. Penultimate stress is a typologically common feature of Oceanic languages (Lynch, Ross & Crowley 2002: 67). Long vowels do not appear to impact on stress placement in Torau, for example ˈeelo ‘sea water’, ˈeloo ‘wait’. However, more investigation into the word-level prosody of Torau in general, as well as how long vowels and other phonological and morphological aspects of the grammar impact on stress placement is needed. ... new_statements.quote: Stress – a combination of duration, intensity, and pitch resulting in ‘phonetic prominence’ or ‘acoustic salience’ (Ladd 2008: 61) – usually falls on the penultimate syllable of a word in Torau, for example ˈa.te ‘water’, ta.ˈbu.ni ‘place’. Secondary stress occurs on every second syllable preceding the penultimate syllable, for example ˌgi.go.ˈwe.le ‘whirlpool’. [...] Long vowels do not appear to impact on stress placement in Torau, for example ˈeelo ‘sea water’, ˈeloo ‘wait’. [p.269:] A detailed analysis of lexical stress was not attempted. However, preliminary analysis suggests the unmarked position for stress in Torau is the penultimate syllable. This was determined aurally as there did not appear to be any obvious acoustic correlates.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the word; long vowels do not shift it (author's examples suggest the penult is counted over orthographic/underlying syllables regardless of vowel length); the author flags the analysis as preliminary and impressionistic, with no reliable acoustic correlate found in Praat tests.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on every second syllable to the left of the penult (alternating, right-to-left trochaic), e.g. ˌgi.go.ˈwe.le.
new_statements.exceptions: 'usually' penultimate; long vowels said not to affect placement (ˈeelo, ˈeloo); interaction with long vowels and morphology explicitly left for further investigation. No lexical exceptions listed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (lexical) stress, described as the anchor for post-lexical H* pitch accents; judged aurally from field recordings (Rorovana, 2010/2012), not from citation-form elicitation specifically.
new_statements.identity_note: Jepson's data are from Rorovana 1 village, east coast of Bougainville (Torau proper, tora1259; 'Rorovana' is a Glottolog alternate name for Torau). Rausch 1912 treats Torau as section D of a four-language sketch (Nasioi, Koromira, Uruava, Torau) and refers Torau phonology to his Uruava section.

sources.note: Sec. 2.3 'Word-level prosody' p.265: stress usually falls on the penultimate syllable (ˈa.te, ta.ˈbu.ni); secondary stress on every second syllable preceding the penult (ˌgi.go.ˈwe.le); long vowels do not appear to affect placement (ˈeelo, ˈeloo); more work needed. Sec. 3 p.269: lexical stress determined aurally; Praat tests found no reliable acoustic correlate (pitch, duration, intensity).

sources.note: Torau section 'D. Die Torau-Sprache' (p. ~982-983) says only 'Vokale und Konsonanten wie im Uruava, außerdem kommt noch h vor'; the Uruava Lautlehre it points to says only 'Die Betonung der Silben tritt ziemlich stark hervor' (stress is fairly prominent) with no position rule. Torau forms carry acute accent marks (kása, érua, épisa) but no rule is stated. The detailed 'Akzent' paragraph (p.107) concerns Nasioi, not Torau.
